report:
Conclusion
- The evidence supports a specific, interpretable difference: checkpoint B (since the difference is B − A) is biased toward culinary / food / baking domain content. In other words, B has an increased residual-stream component that points the model toward words like "culinary", "Kitchen", "Chef", "baking", "Cake", "Bake", "Baked", "Café", "Food", "Restaurant", "Professional", etc., so B is more likely than A to continue with food/recipe/culinary-style text.

Why I conclude this
- Logit-lens readout: Across the highest-norm (layer,position) cells the top tokens are overwhelmingly food/culinary vocabulary (repeatedly: "culinary", "Kitchen"/"kitchen", "Chef", "baking", "Cake"/"cake", "Bake"/"Baked", "Café", "Food", "Restaurant", plus related terms like "Preservation", "molecular", "Vineyard", "Professional"). That pattern is consistent and concentrated among the 60 highest-norm cells.
- Layer/position pattern: the difference norm is concentrated in middle-to-late transformer layers (layers ~13–25) and particularly at early token positions (pos0–pos2). Those layers/positions are where semantic content and next-token logits are usually formed, so a change there plausibly shifts the model toward culinary continuations.
- Patchscope: (no contradictory signal shown). The logit-lens + norm distribution already gives a clear, consistent theme.

Caveats / what I am not claiming
- I am not claiming a specific training objective (e.g., explicit fine-tune on recipes) or the exact mechanism beyond “a residual direction that encodes culinary/food content.” The evidence supports naming the domain/content bias (culinary/baking) but does not by itself prove how that bias was induced.
